fr.elements: Main Building; Detached Structure; Open Green Space; Front Driveway; Access Road; Landscaped Area; Open Terrain; Dense Vegetation; Street Frontage; Perimeter Fencing
fr.considerations: Single Access Point; Long Driveway; Open Terrain; Limited Rear Access; Dense Vegetation
fr.recommendations: Ensuring the single access point and extended driveway remain clear of obstructions at all times could significantly improve emergency responder access and turnaround capability. Visible address marking at the street frontage entrance would support faster navigation to the property. The limited rear access and presence of dense vegetation near structures may affect responder movement around the main building and detached structure, so preserving open pathways between and around both structures could facilitate ground-level access and staging. Identifying and communicating an on-site staging area within the open terrain or green space to local emergency services may also enhance coordination during multi-unit responses.

wildfire.conditions: Scattered Shrubs; Heavy Brush; Scattered Shrubs; Fuel Continuity; Brush Concentration; Mixed Vegetation Cover; Vegetation Adjacent to Structure; Brushland Interface; Open Terrain; Limited Defensible Space; Irrigated Landscape; Single Access Route
wildfire.recommendations: Reducing the concentration of heavy brush and mixed vegetation near the structure should be a priority, as thinning and separating these fuel sources could meaningfully reduce fuel continuity across the property and improve defensible space around improvements. Where shrubs and brush are located immediately adjacent to the structure, increasing the separation between vegetation and exterior surfaces may reduce direct exposure and support suppression operations if needed. The single access route serving the property warrants particular attention — keeping this corridor clear of encroaching vegetation on both sides would support firefighter access and improve evacuation conditions. The brushland interface conditions along the property perimeter suggest that maintaining a managed buffer between dense vegetation and the structure zone could improve long-term wildfire resilience. The irrigated landscaping present on the property is a valuable asset and continuing its maintenance may help reduce fuel availability near the structure. Ongoing management of scattered shrubs throughout the open terrain areas could further reduce fuel continuity across the broader property.
